strengths: The problem setting (target-agnostic calibration under distribution shift) is well motivated and practically relevant; the paper clearly positions FGR against target-domain-aware methods that require target data.

The method is clearly described: DCT/JPEG-style low-pass filtering on a small fraction of training data plus an asymmetric gradient projection treating ID calibration as a first-order hard constraint. The Proposition 4.1 proof (Appendix E) is correct, and the authors are admirably careful to distinguish the projection view from a scalarized weighted-sum objective (Appendix E.3), avoiding a common overclaim.

The evaluation is unusually broad: synthetic (CIFAR-10/100-C, Tiny-ImageNet-C), real-world (Camelyon17, iWildCam, FMoW), semantic shift (Office-Home), multiple architectures (ResNet, DenseNet, WideResNet, ViT, Swin, DeiT), multiple calibration metrics (ECE, CECE, ACE) and post-hoc TS compatibility.

Ablations are thorough and honest: Filter-Only / Rect-Only / Weighted-Sum decomposition (Tables 3-4), comparison against symmetric gradient methods PCGrad/CAGrad, gradient-conflict-rate dynamics (Fig. 6), start-epoch sensitivity (Fig. 7), hyperparameter sensitivity including 2D rho-lambda sweeps, batch-size sensitivity, alternative calibration losses, and a computational cost analysis (18.5% overhead).

The limitations section (Appendix F) is candid: the method is limited to covariate shift in image classification, gains on semantic shift are modest, and it does not address unknown-class OOD detection.
weaknesses: Originality is moderate. Both ingredients are established: JPEG/DCT-style low-pass augmentation and frequency-based robustness arguments (Yin et al. 2019; Wang et al. 2023), and one-sided gradient projection, which is a minor variant of PCGrad-style conflict resolution applied asymmetrically. The contribution is a sensible combination with a calibration-specific application rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

The 'weight-free / no balancing coefficient' simplicity claim is undercut by heavy per-dataset hyperparameter tuning: the focusing parameter gamma is tuned separately for every (dataset, architecture, training-strategy) combination (Tables 9-10, values ranging 1.2-5.5), selected via validation ECE, and lambda is sampled from a curated set. This is comparable in burden to tuning a loss weight, weakening a central selling point.

The theoretical guarantee is weak: it is a standard first-order half-space projection argument, holds only for the exact minibatch gradient, ignores the epsilon stabilizer, and offers no convergence or end-of-training guarantee. The paper is honest about this, but the 'hard constraint with theoretical guarantees' framing in the contributions overstates its practical force.

Results on real-world shifts are mixed rather than dominant: on iWildCam and FMoW, FGR is only marginally better than simpler baselines (e.g., Mixup: 3.50 vs 3.34 ECE on iWildCam; DFL: 26.59 vs 25.06 on FMoW), and on Camelyon17 PCGrad/CAGrad achieve higher test accuracy and better NLL in Table 4. The '40% ACE reduction on Camelyon17' headline is a cherry-picked single number.

Table formatting/units inconsistencies raise readability concerns: CECE values appear on wildly different scales across datasets (e.g., 12.612 on Camelyon17 vs 0.196 on iWildCam), and the abstract's code link is missing/truncated ('available at'), hurting verifiability. One baseline (BSCE-GRA) was reimplemented rather than using official code.
On ID calibration after temperature scaling (Table 14), FGR is not consistently best (e.g., CIFAR-100 DenseNet-121: 3.34 vs DFL 1.51), so the claim of preserving ID performance holds only partially.

The frequency-filtering hypothesis (shifts predominantly alter high-frequency content) is plausible for corruptions but weakly justified for semantic/domain shifts like Office-Home or hospital-level Camelyon17 shifts, where the paper itself acknowledges limited gains; a more rigorous causal analysis connecting filtering to calibration under shift is missing.

strengths: Broad empirical coverage: the method is evaluated on synthetic shifts (CIFAR-10/100-C, Tiny-ImageNet-C), real-world WILDS shifts (Camelyon17, iWildCam, FMoW), a semantic-shift benchmark (Office-Home), and multiple backbones including ViT/Swin/DeiT, which is more comprehensive than typical calibration papers.

Reasonable ablation design: component-wise ablations (Filter Only / Rect. Only / Weighted Sum / FGR), comparison to symmetric multi-objective gradient methods (PCGrad, CAGrad), gradient-conflict-rate analysis, start-epoch sensitivity, batch-size sensitivity, and an explicit training-time overhead analysis (Appendix D.6).

The writing is generally clear, the two-stage fine-tuning variant is a practical addition, and the honest limitations section (Appendix F) appropriately scopes the claims (covariate shift only, limited gains on semantic shift, added compute).

The projection property (Prop. 4.1) is stated carefully at the optimizer level and honestly framed as a one-sided first-order constraint rather than oversold as an equivalence to weighted-sum minimization.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: both components are well-established. DCT/JPEG-style low-pass filtering to remove high-frequency shortcut cues is directly built on prior frequency-robustness work (Yin et al. 2019; Wang et al. 2023; Li et al. 2023), and the rectification rule (Eq. 8) is a one-sided variant of PCGrad's gradient projection onto a half-space. The contribution is a combination of known techniques, and the theoretical result is a straightforward projection calculation.

Internal inconsistencies in reported numbers undermine confidence in the evidence: in Table 1 (bottom), CECE/ACE values appear on a completely different scale than ECE (e.g., iWildCam CECE 0.196 vs ECE 14.99 for CE; Camelyon17 CECE 12.612 vs ECE 12.23), suggesting unit/format errors. In Table 14, several post-temperature-scaling ECE values are larger than the pre-TS values (e.g., Tiny-ImageNet DenseNet-121 CE Post T = 15.01 vs Pre T = 8.26), which contradicts the purpose of temperature scaling and hints at reporting errors.

The headline 'hard constraint / first-order non-increase' guarantee is weak in practice: gcalib is computed on a mini-batch, not the full Dorig, so the guarantee is per-step and per-sample; no evidence is provided on how tight this bound is or how often actual (non-first-order) increases in ID ECE occur.

Gains are not uniformly convincing: AugMix achieves substantially higher accuracy (82.49 vs 75.12 on CIFAR-10-C) with comparable ECE (8.51 vs 9.02), and the Weighted Sum baseline is often within noise of FGR in Table 3 (e.g., Tiny-INet ID/shift ECE 3.02/17.26 vs 2.64/15.46). The paper claims FGR 'substantially' improves calibration, but across many settings improvements over strong baselines (DFL, MaxEnt, BSCE-GRA) are modest.

Results are averaged over only three seeds with no variance or significance testing reported for the main tables, and the focal parameter γ is tuned per dataset/architecture from validation ECE — more tuning burden than the 'weight-free' framing suggests, even if ρ and λ are simple.

The theoretical framing (Section 5.5 conflict-rate discussion) is interpretive rather than validated; the claim that rectification 'prevents overconfidence' during late training is supported only by a correlational plot.
Code availability is stated in the abstract ('Our code is available at') but the link is empty, which harms reproducibility as submitted.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important problem—maintaining calibration under distribution shift without access to target-domain data—with a clear motivation grounded in frequency-domain shortcut learning literature (Yin et al. 2019; Wang et al. 2023).

The method is technically coherent: DCT-based low-pass filtering to suppress high-frequency shortcuts, combined with an asymmetric gradient projection that treats ID calibration as a first-order hard constraint. The framing is carefully distinguished from symmetric multi-objective methods (PCGrad/CAGrad), and Proposition 4.1 with the Appendix E proof correctly characterizes the update as a Euclidean projection onto a half-space.

Evaluation is unusually thorough: synthetic shifts (CIFAR-10/100-C, Tiny-ImageNet-C), real-world WILDS benchmarks (Camelyon17, iWildCam, FMoW), semantic shift (Office-Home), and transformer backbones (ViT, Swin, DeiT). Results are averaged over three seeds and reported across multiple calibration metrics (ECE, CECE, ACE), with and without post-hoc temperature scaling.

The ablations are convincing and address the obvious objections: component-wise ablations (Table 3) show filtering alone degrades ID calibration while rectification alone lacks robustness; comparison against PCGrad/CAGrad (Table 4) shows the asymmetry is doing real work; gradient-conflict-rate analysis (Fig. 6) explains the mechanism; and start-epoch, batch size, γ, ρ, and λ sensitivities are all reported (Figs. 7, 10–13).

Practical considerations are well handled: 18.5% training overhead quantified (Table 19), a two-stage fine-tuning variant that is highly efficient and competitive (Tables 11–13), and compatibility with post-hoc TS demonstrated.
Reproducibility is strong: full pseudocode (Algorithm 1), complete training configurations, baseline hyperparameters and implementation sources, and a stated code release.
The limitations section is honest and specific (covariate-shift scope, no unknown-class OOD detection, modest gains on semantic shift), and the impact statement is appropriate.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate: both ingredients are well-established (frequency filtering for robustness; gradient projection/conflict surgery à la PCGrad). The contribution is primarily the asymmetric constrained formulation applied to calibration, which the paper acknowledges but which limits how fundamental the advance is.

The theoretical guarantee is per-step and first-order only: it ensures L_calib does not increase for a single sufficiently small step under an exact gradient, but with stochastic mini-batch estimates of g_calib, non-SGD optimizers, and 150+ FGR epochs, no end-to-end calibration guarantee follows. The paper is careful about this, but the 'hard constraint' language could still be over-read.

Hyperparameter treatment raises some fairness concerns: γ is tuned per dataset/architecture (Tables 9–10), and the FGR start epoch (200) is a distinctive extra choice not available to baselines; the start-epoch analysis shows results are sensitive to it. Whether baselines received comparable tuning effort is not fully documented.

The guarantee concerns the ID calibration loss (Soft-ECE), not ID accuracy; the claim of preserving ID 'performance' is only empirically supported, and Table 3 shows small accuracy drops in some settings (e.g., CIFAR-10 shift accuracy).

Head-to-head wins are not universal: e.g., on Tiny-ImageNet-C, Mixup achieves better ECE/CECE than FGR (Table 1), on iWildCam PCGrad achieves higher shifted accuracy, and after temperature scaling the gaps narrow considerably (e.g., CIFAR-100-C w/TS: FGR 7.57 vs AugMix 7.84). The advantages are real but dataset-dependent.

The mechanism story (high-frequency shortcuts → overconfidence under shift) is supported by Grad-CAM visualizations and prior work but remains somewhat indirect; no direct experiment ties the calibration gains causally to reduced reliance on high-frequency cues rather than to the regularization effect of the hybrid training distribution alone.
